slides.page_title: Exit Status: The Engine Behind Every Branch

items: `0` = success/true; `1`-`255` = failure/false
Inverted vs C, Python and most languages
`$?` holds the last foreground command's status
The very next command overwrites it — capture now
`if` tests no expression — it runs a command
The branch is taken when that command exits `0`
No `[` needed when a command answers the question
`true` and `false` are real builtins returning 0 and 1

lines: if ! command -v git; then echo missing; fi

items: `test`, `[` and `[[` only produce an exit status
`[` is a command; its last argument must be `]`
`/usr/bin/[` exists — proof it is not syntax
`[[` is the exception: a shell keyword
`&&` runs the right side only after status `0`
`||` runs it only after a non-zero status
`!` negates the status of a whole pipeline
Pipeline status = LAST command; `set -o pipefail` = first failure

blocks.title: Not an if/else
blocks.text: `cmd1 && cmd2 || cmd3` — if `cmd2` fails, `cmd3` runs too. A classic silent bug; write a real `if`.

slides.page_title: Wrapper Scripts That Report False Success

blocks.title: Wrappers Must Not Lie
blocks.text: Ending a wrapper with `echo done` returns `0` even after the real command failed — CI, `set -e` and `&&` all read that as success.

slides.page_title: case Dispatch and Propagating a Script's Status

items: A long `if/elif` chain on one value flattens into `case`
`restart)` simply reuses the other two branches
A script's own status is its ==last command's== status
`exit "$rc"` hands the child's status to the caller

slides.page_title: Exit Codes, test Operators and File Checks

items: Numeric: `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge`, numbers only
`=` and `!=` are for strings only
Mixing the two families compares the wrong thing

lines: while ! nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done

blocks.title: set -e Blind Spots
items: Suppressed inside `if`, `while`, `until` conditions
Suppressed after `&&`, `||` and `!`
That is why a failing test never kills the script
Trap: a function whose last command fails returns non-zero too
`[ EXPR ]` — spaces around `[` and `]` are mandatory
`[$x = 1]` is a command-not-found error
`[` is the command, `]` its required last argument
`-e` follows symlinks, `-L` does not
A broken symlink is `-L` true but `-e` false
`-nt` newer, `-ot` older, `-ef` same inode
`[ "$f" = *.txt ]` compares to the literal `*.txt`
Pattern matching belongs to `[[ ]]` or `case`

blocks.title: Which Bracket
blocks.text: Shebang `#!/bin/sh` or dash: `[ ]` with every variable quoted. Shebang `#!/bin/bash`: reach for `[[ ]]`.

items: An unquoted empty variable collapses the word away
`[ $x = y ]` with `x` empty becomes `[ = y ]`
`[ ]` word-splits and globs unquoted variables
A variable holding `a b` arrives as two arguments

blocks.title: Old-Script Idioms
items: `[ "x$x" = "xy" ]` predates reliable quoting
`[ "$x" = "-n" ]` misparses in ancient shells
Portable AND: `[ a ] && [ b ]`
`-a` / `-o` are deprecated and ambiguous
Bash parses `[[ ]]` specially — expansion rules suspended
No word splitting, no globbing on variables
`[[ $x = y ]]` is safe when `x` is empty or has spaces
Cannot go where a command is needed, e.g. `find -exec`
`==` / `!=` glob-match: `[[ $name == a* ]]`
A quoted right side is literal: `[[ $f == "*.txt" ]]`
`=~` takes an ERE, not PCRE, and must be UNQUOTED
Capture groups land in the `BASH_REMATCH` array

blocks.title: Escape Quoting Hell
blocks.text: Store a complex regex in a variable and use it bare. Quoting `$re` turns the pattern back into a literal string.

items: `<` and `>` compare strings, no backslash escaping
`-eq` / `-lt` still work, but `(( ))` is the better choice

slides.page_title: Choosing a Bracket, Then Arithmetic with (( ))

blocks.title: Rules of Thumb
items: Left side: quoting never needed
Right side unquoted = pattern; quoted = literal
`${BASH_REMATCH[1]}` is the first capture group
`(( expr ))` evaluates and sets an exit status
`$(( expr ))` is EXPANSION: substitutes the result
Variables need no `$` inside: `(( i < n ))`
`$` is allowed there but only adds noise

blocks.title: Inverted Truth
blocks.text: A numeric result of `0` gives exit status `1` (false); non-zero gives status `0` (true). The opposite of everywhere else — memorise it.

items: Ternary `? :`, logical `&& || !`
Bitwise `& | ^ << >>`
Real chaining: `(( a < b && b < c ))`
`$(( 7 / 2 ))` is `3` — truncating division
`$(( 1.5 ))` is a syntax error; use `bc -l` or `awk`
`$(( -7 % 3 ))` is `-1`, truncated toward zero
Overflow wraps at 64-bit signed, silently, no error

lines: echo $(( 08 + 1 )) # value too great for base

items: Bites date math: `08` and `09` are invalid octal digits

lines: (( i++ ))     # status 1 kills a set -e script

items: Post-increment returns the OLD value's truthiness
`let 'x = 1 + 2'` and `declare -i x` are older forms
`(( ))` is the modern idiom — prefer it

slides.page_title: for Loops: Word Lists, Globs and Ranges

blocks.title: Guard Idiom
blocks.text: `if (( count > 0 )); then` reads better and is safer than `[ "$count" -gt 0 ]`.

items: `for x in a b c` iterates words after expansion
An empty list means zero iterations, status `0`
The loop returns its last body command's status

lines: for x in a b c; do echo "$x"; done
for f in *.txt; do wc -l "$f"; done
for arg in "$@"; do echo "$arg"; done
for arg; do echo "$arg"; done  # same thing

items: `for f in *.txt` is SAFE with spaces in filenames
`for f in $(ls)` word-splits and breaks on newlines
Never parse `ls` — the glob already did the work

blocks.title: Empty Glob
blocks.text: With no matches, `*.txt` stays literal and the body runs once on the pattern itself. Guard with `[[ -e $f ]]` or `shopt -s nullglob`.

items: `for x in "${arr[@]}"` — quotes and `[@]` both required
`${arr[*]}` joins everything into one word
`{1..$n}` fails: braces expand before parameters

lines: for i in {1..10}; do echo $i; done
for i in {0..20..5}; do echo $i; done
for (( i=0; i<n; i++ )); do echo $i; done

items: `for (( i=0; i<n; i++ ))` is arithmetic context, no `$`
The best form for counters and variable bounds
`break` exits, `continue` skips; `break 2` exits two loops
`for line in $(cat f)` splits on every space, not per line
`IFS=$'\n'` narrows splitting but still globs
Both stay inferior to `while IFS= read -r line`

blocks.title: Redirect the Whole Loop
items: Loops are compound commands
`for ...; do ...; done > out.txt` opens the file once
Beats reopening it inside the body each pass
The condition is a command list, not an expression
`while [[ $i -lt 5 ]]`, `while (( i < 5 ))`, `while ping -c1 h`
`until` is just `while !` — pick the positive reading

lines: while (( i<5 )); do echo $i; (( i++ )); done
while :; do :; done      # ':' is the no-op

items: Multi-command condition: only the LAST status decides
`while cmd1; cmd2; do` branches on `cmd2`
`break` / `continue` work as in `for`, with level counts

blocks.title: Always Sleep When Polling
blocks.text: A bare `while ! test; do :; done` pins one CPU core at 100%. The `sleep` in a polling loop is mandatory, not decoration.

items: Infinite-loop bug: forgetting to mutate the counter
Or mutating a copy inside a subshell — lost on exit
`while read` consumes stdin; body commands fight for it

blocks.title: Stdin Thieves
items: `ssh`, `ffmpeg` and `mysql` eat the loop's input
The loop then exits after one iteration
Fix with `ssh -n`, or `< /dev/null` on the command

slides.page_title: read Line by Line and the Subshell Trap

items: `read VAR` pulls ==one line== from stdin into `VAR`
It returns non-zero at EOF — that is what ends the loop
`-r` keeps `\` literal; without it, backslashes vanish
An `IFS=` prefix stops leading/trailing space being trimmed
`IFS=` is a **per-command** assignment, not a global change
Split fields instead: `IFS=: read -r user pw rest`
A final line with no newline needs `|| [[ -n $line ]]`

lines: grep x f | while read l; do
blocks.note: the pipe forks the loop into a subshell
process substitution keeps the body here

blocks.title: Past One Line at a Time
items: `mapfile -t arr < file` slurps the whole file at once
`read -t S` times out, `-n N` reads chars, `-d ''` reads to NUL
NUL-safe lists: `find . -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f`
A second file needs its own fd: `exec 3< b.txt` then `read -u 3`
A quoted pattern is literal: `"*"` means an asterisk
Otherwise patterns match the expanded word directly
`shopt -s extglob` adds `@(a|b) ?(x) *(x) +(x) !(x)`

slides.page_title: case: Patterns, Terminators and Final Pitfalls

items: `$var` needs no quotes — no splitting in the case word
Same protection you get inside `[[ ]]`
First matching pattern wins; no fallthrough by default
No `break` needed — `;;` ends each branch
`*)` must be **LAST** — a mid-list catch-all kills the rest
A missing `;;` is a syntax error at the next `)`
`shopt -s nocasematch` makes matching case-insensitive
Status = last command in the branch; `0` if none matched
`if [$x -eq 1]` — `[$x` is not a command
`[ "$a" == "$b" ]` is Bash-only; `dash` errors on it
`if cmd > /dev/null` tests status, **not** output
Dropping `-r` from `read` mangles paths and escapes

blocks.title: Defensive Header
blocks.text: Open real scripts with `set -euo pipefail` and `IFS=$'\n\t'`. Check syntax with `bash -n`, trace with `bash -x`, and let ==shellcheck== catch the rest.

caption.text: `[[ 10 > 9 ]]` is false, and that one line has broken more deploy scripts than any missing semicolon. This handbook walks the whole branching surface of Bash — exit status as the real engine, `[` vs `[[` vs `(( ))`, for/while/until/case, and the single correct way to read a file line by line. Ten pages of dense field notes, plus the gotchas that corrupt scripts without ever printing an error.
